title: Demonstratives: este, esse, aquele
summary: Point to things near you, near the listener, or farther away with este, esse, and aquele families.

sections.heading: The three distances
sections.body:
Demonstratives agree in gender and number. In everyday Brazil, **esse/essa** often covers many situations, but the three-way contrast is useful.

| Distance | Masculine | Feminine | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| near me | este(s) | esta(s) | this/these |
| near you / already mentioned | esse(s) | essa(s) | that/those |
| far from both | aquele(s) | aquela(s) | that/those over there |

examples.en: That house over there is old.

sections.heading: Neutral forms: isto, isso, aquilo
sections.body: Use **isto**, **isso**, and **aquilo** when you do not name the noun or when referring to an idea, situation, or unknown thing. They do not change for gender or number.

sections.heading: In conversation and text
sections.body: In conversation, **esse/essa/isso** are very common. In writing, **este** can refer to what comes next, while **esse** can refer back to what was already mentioned.

examples.pt: Tenho esta dúvida: como usar crase?
examples.en: I have this question: how do you use crase?

examples.pt: Crase é difícil. Essa dúvida é comum.
examples.en: Crase is hard. That question is common.

keyPoints: Demonstratives agree with the noun: este livro, esta casa, estes livros.
Isto/isso/aquilo are neutral and do not modify a noun.
Esse/essa/isso are extremely common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese.
Aquele/aquela points to something distant in space, time, or memory.

commonMistakes.note: Use este/esse/aquele before nouns, not isto/isso/aquilo.
